en: The Path of Discrimination,
Chapter on the Coupling, 2.9.
Discourse on the Powers (Balakathā)
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these five powers.
What are the five?
The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration,
and the power of wisdom— these, monks,
are the five powers. Moreover, there are sixty-eight powers:
The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, the power of wisdom, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of reflection,
the power of cultivation, the power of blamelessness, the power of gathering, the power of patience, the power of designation, the power of self-dedication,
the power of sovereignty, the power of resolution, the power of serenity, the power of insight— ten.

“There are the five powers of one in training, the ten powers of one beyond training, the ten powers of one whose taints are destroyed, the ten powers of supernormal success, and the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
What is the power of faith?
It is the power of faith because it does not waver in the face of lack of faith.
The power of faith is so called in the sense of supporting co-nascent states; the power of faith is so called in the sense of exhausting the defilements;
the power of faith is so called in the sense of purifying penetration and so forth; the power of faith is so called in the sense of the mind’s resolution;
the power of faith is so called in the sense of the mind’s cleansing; the power of faith is so called in the sense of the attainment of distinction; [and] in the sense of further penetration.
The power of faith: the power of faith in the sense of the clear realization of truth; the power of faith in the sense of establishing [the mind] in cessation.
This is the power of faith.
What is the power of energy?
"It does not waver in laziness"—this is the power of energy (*vīriyabala*).
The power of energy is so called in the sense of providing support for co-arisen states; in the sense of the total exhaustion of the defilements;
in the sense of purification through penetration and so forth; and in the sense of the mind's determination.
The power of energy in the sense of purification of the mind; the power of energy in the sense of attaining distinction; the power of energy in the sense of higher penetration;
the power of energy in the sense of the realization of the truths; the power of energy in the sense of establishing [the mind] in cessation.
This is the power of energy.
What is the power of mindfulness?
It is the power of mindfulness because it does not waver in negligence.
The power of mindfulness is so called in the sense of supporting co-arisen states …pe…
The power of mindfulness is so called in the sense of establishing [the mind] in cessation.
This is the power of mindfulness.
What is the power of concentration?
"It does not waver through restlessness" refers to the power of concentration.
The power of concentration is so called in the sense of providing support for co-nascent states; ... [and so on] ...
it is the power of concentration in the sense of establishing them in cessation.
This is the power of concentration.
What is the power of wisdom?
It does not waver because of ignorance—this is the power of wisdom.
The power of wisdom, in the sense of supporting co-arisen states … [and so on] … the power of wisdom,
in the sense of establishing [them] in cessation.
This is the power of wisdom.
What is the power of moral shame?
One feels shame because of renunciation for sensual desire;
this is the power of moral shame.
One feels shame for ill will because of non-ill will; this is the power of moral shame.
One feels shame for sloth and torpor because of the perception of light; this is the power of moral shame.
One feels shame for restlessness because of non-distraction; this is the power of moral shame.
Doubt is put to shame by the discernment of phenomena; this is the power of moral shame.
Ignorance is put to shame by knowledge; this is the power of moral shame.
Discontent is put to shame by gladness; this is the power of moral shame.
One feels shame regarding the hindrances by means of the first jhāna—this is the power of moral shame.
…pe… One feels shame regarding all defilements by means of the path to arahantship—this is the power of moral shame.
This is the power of moral shame.
What is the power of moral dread? One dreads sensual desire through renunciation—this is the power of moral dread.
One dreads ill will through non-ill will—this is the power of moral dread.
Through the perception of light, sloth and torpor are shunned—this is the power of moral dread.
Through non-distraction, restlessness is shunned—this is the power of moral dread.
Through the discernment of phenomena, doubt is shunned—this is the power of moral dread.
One shrinks away from ignorance by means of knowledge:
this is the power of moral dread. One shrinks away from discontent by means of gladness: this is the power of moral dread.
One shrinks away from the hindrances by means of the first jhāna: this is the power of moral dread... [and so on].
The power of moral dread is that by which one is made to shrink away from all defilements through the path of arahantship.
This is the power of moral dread.
What is the power of reflective contemplation?
"One reflects upon sensual desire by means of renunciation"—this is the power of reflection.
"One reflects upon ill will by means of non-ill will"—this is the power of reflection.
"One reflects upon sloth and torpor by means of the perception of light"—this is the power of reflection.
One reflects upon restlessness through non-distraction: this is the power of reflection.
One reflects upon doubt through the discernment of phenomena: this is the power of reflection.
One reflects upon ignorance through knowledge: this is the power of reflection.
"By means of gladness, one reflects upon discontent": this is the power of reflection.
"By means of the first jhāna, one reflects upon the hindrances":
this is the power of reflection …pe… "By means of the path of arahantship, one reflects upon all defilements": this is the power of reflection.
This is the power of reflection.
What is the power of development?
Abandoning sensual desire, one develops renunciation—this is the power of development.
"Abandoning ill will, one develops non-ill will"—this is the power of development.
"Abandoning sloth and torpor, one develops the perception of light"—this is the power of development.
"Abandoning restlessness, one develops non-distraction"—this is the power of development.
Abandoning doubt, one develops the discernment of phenomena—this is the power of development.
Abandoning ignorance, one develops knowledge—this is the power of development.
Abandoning aversion, one develops gladness—this is the power of development.
"One who abandons the hindrances develops the first jhāna"—this is the power of development. ...
[and so on] ... "One who abandons all defilements develops the path of arahantship"—this is the power of development.
This is the power of development.
What is the power of blamelessness?
Because sensual desire has been abandoned, there is nothing blameworthy in renunciation—this is the power of blamelessness.
Because ill will has been abandoned, there is nothing blameworthy in non-ill will—this is the power of blamelessness.
Because sloth and torpor have been abandoned, there is no fault in the perception of light—this is the power of blamelessness.
Because restlessness has been abandoned, there is no fault in non-distraction—this is the power of blamelessness.
Because doubt has been abandoned, there is no fault in the discernment of phenomena—this is the power of blamelessness.
Because ignorance has been abandoned, there is nothing blameworthy in knowledge—this is the power of blamelessness.
Because discontent has been abandoned, there is nothing blameworthy in gladness—this is the power of blamelessness.
Because the hindrances have been abandoned, there is nothing blameworthy in the first jhāna—this is the power of blamelessness … [and so on] …
Because all defilements have been abandoned, there is no fault whatsoever in the path of arahantship—this is the power of blamelessness (*anavajjabala*).
This is the power of blamelessness.
What is the power of conciliation (*saṅgahabala*)?
Abandoning sensual desire, one gathers the mind by means of renunciation: this is the power of gathering.
Abandoning ill will, one gathers the mind by means of non-ill will: this is the power of gathering.
Abandoning sloth and torpor, one gathers the mind by means of the perception of light: this is the power of gathering... [and so on].
Abandoning all defilements, one gathers the mind by means of the path to arahantship; this is the power of gathering.
This is the power of gathering.
What is the power of patience?
Because sensual desire has been abandoned, renunciation is acceptable; this is the power of patience.
Because ill will has been abandoned, non-ill will is acceptable; this is the power of patience.
Because sloth and torpor have been abandoned, the perception of light is acceptable; this is the power of patience.
Because restlessness has been abandoned, non-distraction is acceptable—this is the power of acceptance.
Because doubt has been abandoned, the discernment of phenomena is acceptable—this is the power of acceptance.
Because ignorance has been abandoned, knowledge is acceptable—this is the power of acceptance.
Because discontent has been abandoned, joy is acceptable—this is the power of patience.
Because the hindrances have been abandoned, the first jhāna is acceptable—this is the power of patience.
… [and so on] … because all defilements have been abandoned, the path of arahantship is acceptable—this is the power of patience.
This is the power of patience.
What is the power of resolution?
One who abandons sensual desire resolves the mind upon renunciation—this is the power of resolution.
The power of discernment (*paññattibala*).
Abandoning ill will, one discerns the mind by way of non-ill will—this is the power of discernment.
Abandoning sloth and torpor, one discerns the mind by way of the perception of light—this is the power of discernment... [and so on].
Abandoning all defilements, one makes the mind manifest by means of the path of arahantship; this is the power of manifestation (*paññattibala*).
This is the power of manifestation.
What is the power of self-ownership (*nijjhattibala*)?
Abandoning sensual desire, one gladdens the mind by means of renunciation; this is the power of gladdening (*nijjhatti-bala*).
Abandoning ill will, one gladdens the mind by means of non-ill will; this is the power of gladdening.
Abandoning sloth and torpor, one gladdens the mind by means of the perception of light; this is the power of gladdening... [and so on].
Abandoning all defilements, one causes the mind to be purified by means of the path of arahantship;
this is the power of purification (*nijjhatti-bala*).
What is the power of mastery (*issariya-bala*)?
Abandoning sensual desire, one brings the mind under control by means of renunciation; this is the power of mastery.
Abandoning ill will, one brings the mind under control by means of non-ill will; this is the power of mastery.
Abandoning sloth and torpor, one brings the mind under control by means of the perception of light; this is the power of mastery... [and so on].
Abandoning all defilements, one exercises mastery over the mind by means of the path of arahantship;
this is the power of mastery.
What is the power of resolution?
Abandoning sensual desire, one resolves the mind by means of renunciation: this is the power of resolution.
Abandoning ill will, one resolves the mind by means of non-ill will: this is the power of resolution.
Abandoning sloth and torpor, one resolves the mind by means of the perception of light: this is the power of resolution... [and so on].
Abandoning all defilements, one resolves the mind by means of the path of arahantship;
this is the power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhānabala*).
What is the power of serenity (*samathabala*)?
One-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of renunciation is the power of serenity; one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of non-ill will is the power of serenity;

one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of the perception of light is the power of serenity … [and so on] … one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of breathing in while contemplating relinquishment is the power of serenity; one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of breathing out while contemplating relinquishment is the power of serenity.
In what sense is it called the "power of serenity"?
By means of the first jhāna, one is unshaken by the hindrances—this is the power of serenity.
By means of the second jhāna, one is unshaken by applied and sustained thought—this is the power of serenity.
By means of the third jhāna, one is unshaken by rapture—this is the power of serenity.
By means of the fourth jhāna, one is unshaken by pleasure and pain—this is the power of serenity (samathabala).
By means of the attainment of the base of infinite space, one is unshaken by the perception of form, the perception of sensory reaction, and the perception of diversity—this is the power of serenity.
By means of the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, one is unshaken by the perception of the base of infinite space—this is the power of serenity.
It is not shaken by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness when in the attainment of the base of nothingness: this is the power of serenity.
It is not shaken by the perception of the base of nothingness when in the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: this is the power of serenity.
It is not shaken, does not waver, and is not disturbed by restlessness, by the defilements associated with restlessness, or by the aggregates: this is the power of serenity.
This is the power of serenity.
What is the power of insight?
Contemplation of impermanence is the power of insight; contemplation of suffering is the power of insight … [and so on] …

The power of insight is the contemplation of relinquishment; the power of insight is the contemplation of impermanence in form; the power of insight is the contemplation of suffering in form …pe… the power of insight is the contemplation of relinquishment in form; [and so on] for feeling …pe… for perception …
In volitional formations … in consciousness … in the eye … [and so on] … up to … [the six internal and external bases] … in aging-and-death.

Contemplation of impermanence in aging-and-death is the power of insight; contemplation of suffering in aging-and-death is the power of insight …pe… contemplation of relinquishment in aging-and-death is the power of insight.
In what sense is it called the "power of insight"?
It does not waver from the perception of permanence due to the contemplation of impermanence: this is the power of insight.
It does not waver from the perception of pleasure due to the contemplation of suffering: this is the power of insight.
It does not waver from the perception of self due to the contemplation of non-self: this is the power of insight.
It does not waver from delight through the contemplation of disenchantment—this is the power of insight.
It does not waver from lust through the contemplation of dispassion—this is the power of insight.
It does not waver from origination through the contemplation of cessation—this is the power of insight.
"It does not waver in grasping through the contemplation of relinquishment"—this is the power of insight.
"It does not waver, does not shake, and does not tremble before ignorance and the defilements associated with ignorance, nor before the aggregates"—this is the power of insight.
This is the power of insight.
What are the ten powers of one in training and the ten powers of one beyond training?
One trains in right view, thus it is a power of one in training.
Because of having trained therein, it is a power of one beyond training.
"He trains in right intention" is the power of training;
because he has trained therein,
it is the power of one beyond training.
Right speech … right action … right livelihood …
right effort … right mindfulness … right concentration …
"One trains in right knowledge ... [and] in right liberation"—this is the power of one in training.
Because of having trained therein:
The power of one beyond training.
These are the ten powers of one in training and the ten powers of one beyond training.
What are the ten powers of one whose taints are destroyed?
In this case, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, all conditioned phenomena have been clearly seen as they really are with right wisdom as impermanent.
That a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed has clearly seen all conditioned phenomena as they really are with right wisdom as impermanent is also a power of that bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed,
by virtue of which power the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed—
He claims the destruction of the taints, saying: “The taints are destroyed in me.
Furthermore, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, sensual pleasures have been clearly seen as they really are with correct wisdom, like a pit of glowing embers.
That a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed has clearly seen sensual pleasures as they really are with correct wisdom, like a pit of glowing embers...
This too is a power of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints: "My taints are destroyed.

Furthermore, the mind of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed slants, slopes, and inclines toward seclusion; it is withdrawn, delights in renunciation, and has become entirely free from states that are the basis for the taints.
That a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed has a mind inclined toward seclusion, sloping toward seclusion, leaning toward seclusion,
established in seclusion, delighting in renunciation, and entirely freed from states that provide a basis for the taints—
this too is a power of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed realizes the destruction of the taints.
He declares: “My taints are destroyed.
Furthermore, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed.
That the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed—this too [is a quality of one whose taints are destroyed].
A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed possesses a power by virtue of which that bhikkhu with destroyed taints claims the destruction of the taints, saying: “My taints are destroyed.
Furthermore, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the four right strivings have been developed and well developed... [as before] ...
The four bases of psychic power have been developed, well developed;
... the five faculties have been developed, well developed;
... the five powers have been developed, well developed.
The seven factors of enlightenment have been developed, well-developed...
[and so on] ...the noble eightfold path has been developed, well-developed.
That the noble eightfold path has been developed, well-developed by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed—this too belongs to one whose taints are destroyed.
This is the power of a bhikkhu, by relying upon which power a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed declares the destruction of the taints: “My taints are destroyed.
These are the ten powers of one whose taints are destroyed.
What are the ten powers of supernormal success?
Success by resolution, success by transformation, success consisting of mind-made [form], success through the exercise of knowledge, success through the exercise of concentration,
noble success, success born of the ripening of kamma, success belonging to one possessed of merit, success consisting of science,
and success in various instances by way of right application in the sense of succeeding.
These are the ten powers of psychic potency.
What are the ten powers of a Tathāgata?
Here, a Tathāgata understands, as it really is, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible—
this too is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma—past, future, and present—in terms of its basis and its cause.

That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma—past, future, and present—in terms of its basis and its cause: this too is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which the Tathāgata...
He claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the practice leading everywhere.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the practice leading everywhere—this too is a quality of the Tathāgata.
There is the power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands the world with its many and diverse elements as it really is.
That the Tathāgata understands the world with its many elements and its various elements as it really is—this too is a quality of the Tathāgata...
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands the diversity of the inclinations of beings as it really is.
That the Tathāgata understands the diversity of the inclinations of beings as it really is—this too is a quality of the Tathāgata...
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the degrees of the faculties of other beings and other individuals.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the degrees of the faculties of other beings and other individuals—this too is a quality of the Tathāgata...
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the defilement, the purification, and the emergence regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.

Furthermore, in that the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the defilement, the purification, and the emergence regarding the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments—this too is a quality of the Tathāgata...
Furthermore, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say:
one birth, two births... [and so on].
Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.
That the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past lives is as follows:
One birth, two births …pe… this too is a Tathāgata’s …pe….
Furthermore, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn …pe….
Furthermore, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn...
[as before] ...this too is a quality of the Tathāgata...

Furthermore, through the destruction of the taints, the Tathāgata dwells having realized for himself, through direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.

Furthermore, that the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, remains therein— this too is a power of the Tathāgata,
by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies.
He sets in motion the Wheel of Brahma.
These are the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
In what sense is it the power of faith?
In what sense is it the power of energy?
In what sense is it the power of mindfulness?
In what sense is it the power of concentration?
In what sense is it the power of wisdom?
In what sense is it the power of moral shame?
In what sense is it the power of moral dread?
In what sense is it the power of reflection?
… [and so on] … In what sense is it the power of a Tathāgata?
It is the power of faith in the sense of being unshakable by lack of faith.
The power of energy is in the sense of being unshakable by laziness;
the power of mindfulness is in the sense of being unshakable by negligence;
the power of concentration is in the sense of being unshakable by restlessness.
The power of wisdom is in the sense of being unshakable by ignorance.
One feels shame regarding evil, unwholesome states—this is the power of moral shame.
One feels dread regarding evil, unwholesome states—this is the power of moral dread.
"By means of knowledge, one reflects upon the defilements"—this is the power of reflection.
"The states born therein have a single flavor"—this is the power of development.
"In that there is nothing blameworthy"—this is the power of blamelessness.
"By means of that, he gathers the mind together"— this is the power of gathering. "That is acceptable to him"—
this is the power of patience.
By means of that, one makes the mind known—this is the power of designation (paññatti-bala).
By means of that, one causes the mind to reflect—this is the power of reflection (nijjhatti-bala).
By means of that, one brings the mind under control—this is the power of mastery (issariya-bala).
“He resolves the mind with that” is the power of resolution.
“The mind becomes one-pointed by means of that” is the power of serenity.
“He contemplates the phenomena arisen therein” is the power of insight.
In that regard, one trains— this is the power of training.
Because of having trained in that— this is the power of one beyond training.
"By him the taints are exhausted"—this is the power of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava-bala*).
"It succeeds for him"—this is the power of spiritual success (*iddhi-bala*).
"In the sense of being immeasurable, it is the power of a Tathāgata."
The Discourse on Strength is finished.
